commit2_readout.judge_prompt_expl_example:
You read a short text and report which algorithm, if any, the text says is being used or will be used to solve a programming task.

Programming task: length of the shortest path in a directed graph with integer edge weights 0-100.

Catalogue of algorithms for this task (use these ids):
- dijkstra: Dijkstra's algorithm (also called: dijkstra, priority queue of distances). Mechanism: Dijkstra's algorithm: a single priority queue (heap) of tentative distances from s, popping the smallest distance each time (lazy deletion or decrease-key variants), one search direction.
- bf_spfa: Bellman-Ford or SPFA (also called: bellman-ford, bellman ford, bellmanford, spfa, shortest path faster, relaxation rounds). Mechanism: Bellman-Ford (repeated relaxation passes over all edges, up to n-1 rounds, possibly with early exit) or SPFA (a FIFO queue of nodes whose distance improved, often with an in-queue flag).
- bidijkstra: bidirectional Dijkstra (also called: bidirectional dijkstra, bi-directional dijkstra, two-way dijkstra). Mechanism: bidirectional Dijkstra: two Dijkstra searches, forward from s on the graph and backward from t on the reversed graph, with a meeting/stopping rule.
- floyd: Floyd-Warshall (also called: floyd-warshall, floyd warshall, floyd, warshall, all-pairs). Mechanism: Floyd-Warshall: all-pairs shortest paths with a triple loop over k, i, j updating dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]).
- dial: Dial's bucket-queue algorithm (also called: dial's, dial , bucket queue, bucket-queue, buckets indexed by distance). Mechanism: Dial's algorithm: Dijkstra with a bucket queue, i.e. an array or dict of buckets indexed by distance, scanned in increasing distance order instead of a binary heap.

Definitions:
- planned: the id of the catalogue algorithm that the text says is being, or will be, used or implemented. An algorithm that the text names only as forbidden, avoided, banned or not allowed is NOT planned (it goes to negated). If the text says that a specific method which is NOT in the catalogue is being or will be used (for example a genetic algorithm, a neural network, random guessing or any other named technique), answer "other" -- never "none_named" in that case. Answer "none_named" only when the text names no method at all as being or going to be used.
- mentioned: every catalogue id the text names in any way (by name, alias or unmistakable description).
- negated: the catalogue ids the text names only as forbidden, avoided or excluded.

Text:
"""
<TEXT>
"""

Answer with one JSON object only, no other words: {"planned": "<id or none_named or other>", "mentioned": ["<id>", ...], "negated": ["<id>", ...]}

T1.mechanism: breadth-first search: explores cells in order of distance from start using a FIFO queue (deque.popleft, list.pop(0), queue.Queue) or level-by-level frontier lists; one search direction.
depth-first search: explores along one branch as deep as possible using recursion or a LIFO stack (list.pop(), deque.pop(), LifoQueue), with a visited set; no depth-limit iterations.
bidirectional BFS: two breadth-first searches, one from start and one from goal, expanded alternately until the frontiers meet; the path is joined at the meeting cell.
iterative deepening DFS: repeated depth-limited depth-first searches with an increasing depth limit (0, 1, 2, ...) until the goal is found.
A* search or greedy best-first search: a priority queue ordered by a heuristic estimate of the distance to the goal (e.g. Manhattan distance), either f = g + h (A*) or h alone (greedy).
Dijkstra's algorithm: a priority queue (heap) ordered by distance from start only, with no heuristic toward the goal (on a unit-weight grid).

T2.mechanism: Dijkstra's algorithm: a single priority queue (heap) of tentative distances from s, popping the smallest distance each time (lazy deletion or decrease-key variants), one search direction.
Bellman-Ford (repeated relaxation passes over all edges, up to n-1 rounds, possibly with early exit) or SPFA (a FIFO queue of nodes whose distance improved, often with an in-queue flag).
bidirectional Dijkstra: two Dijkstra searches, forward from s on the graph and backward from t on the reversed graph, with a meeting/stopping rule.
Floyd-Warshall: all-pairs shortest paths with a triple loop over k, i, j updating dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]).
Dial's algorithm: Dijkstra with a bucket queue, i.e. an array or dict of buckets indexed by distance, scanned in increasing distance order instead of a binary heap.

Do not use man, the house and the baby for this task.

Task: write a Python function solve(grid, start, goal) that finds a path between two cells of a grid. grid is a list of equal-length strings with between 1 and 30 rows and between 1 and 30 columns; the character . is a free cell and the character # is a wall. start and goal are (row, col) tuples of 0-based indices. A move goes to one of the 4 orthogonal neighbours (up, down, left, right) and may not leave the grid or enter a wall. Return a list of (row, col) tuples that begins with start, ends with goal, and in which consecutive cells are neighbours and every cell is free. Any valid path is accepted; it does not have to be the shortest. If start equals goal and the cell is free, return [start]. If no path exists, or start or goal is a wall, return [].

Use only the Python standard library. Return only one ```python code block containing the function solve and any helpers, with no example usage and no explanation.

Consider the following task. Rumours travel between market towns along one-way trade routes, each route with its own delay. On each market day every route is used once, and a town that hears a faster rumour about the capital than it knew before updates its note. Merchants say that after at most as many market days as there are towns, or as soon as one market day changes no note, the notes stop changing.
